rationale: Defined minority with severe residual CF pathophysiology: 2434 ineligible by age or genotype; 1226 ineligible adolescents/adults with data. Not a large share of the 33989 Registry but the clinical gap for those people is classic untreated-like CFTR failure.
No approved mutation-agnostic CFTR restoration therapy. Modulators require protein production. This is the cleanest remaining causal gap.
Reviewed map shows high industry crowding: gene therapy mRNA ASO anion-bypass and preclinical genetic listings. 13 industry investigational crowding units. Many well-resourced active programs.

Biology and endpoints are clear (sweat chloride FEV1). Therapeutic precedent exists for CFTR restoration in protein-producing genotypes. Lung delivery of nucleic acids is still the hard part but several modalities are already in human studies.
Lifelong severe disease with orphan-drug and modulator-era payer precedent. Addressable US count is small; do not treat 2434 as a TAM.

Inhaled mRNA AAV and related delivery are in active CF trials in this snapshot. Failed historical readthrough (ataluren) is a lesson not a current competitor. Alyftrek still leaves a genotype-ineligible group.
623 people aged 12+ in 2020 with no CFTRm prescription 2022-2024. CFF notes milder sweat chloride and lower care utilization so this is not equivalent to N1.
Highly effective modulators are approved and widely prescribed (87.5% of ages 12+). The residual gap is access tolerability and preference not absence of a disease-modifying class.
Next-gen modulators are an industry race (Sionna plus Vertex HV studies) on top of an approved HEMT franchise. Several well-resourced programs; not empty.
The intervention class is proven. Remaining questions are tolerability formulation and who among the 623 actually needs a new product versus care-delivery support.
Mixed milder phenotype plus specialty-pharmacy friction that is hypothesized not measured in public patient-level data.
Sionna and Vertex are already running the next-gen modulator programs. A new company would enter a defined incumbent race rather than a newly opened window.
IV-treated PEx 12.1% (was 35.8% in 2009). Mean FEV1 89.1% overall vs 72.8% ages 40-49. 61 lung transplants (was 249 in 2019). Residual pulmonary disease is smaller than pre-HEMT and not zero.
Airway clearance mucolytics and anti-inflammatories exist. Residual exacerbations and advanced disease on HEMT mean options are partial not absent.

No reviewed industry CF-specific investigational anti-inflammatory after excluding NCFB DPP1 programs. Late-stage crowding exists in the adjacent NCFB indication (brensocatib-class) which the rubric treats as a 3 not a 5.

FEV1 and PEx endpoints exist. Residual disease after HEMT is mixed (infection structure inflammation) so a single CF-specific anti-inflammatory bet is messier than pre-modulator inflammation programs.
Chronic inhaled therapies and residual PEx treatment days (median 14 among those with at least one PEx) are costly. Still not a TAM build.
HEMT creates a new residual-disease question. Translation from NCFB DPP1 success into CF is unproven and could close the window as easily as open it.
PA 23.3% of cultured (was 52.0% in 2009). NTM 11.6% of mycobacterial cultures and 18.7% among ages 60+. Fewer cultures since 2020 affect ascertainment.
Inhaled tobramycin aztreonam and azithromycin exist. Chronic PA and NTM persist. Novel modalities (phage gallium) are early.
Reviewed industry investigational crowding is low (BX004). Approved inhaled antibiotics occupy SoC. AP-PA02 had no matching active CF-like trial. Few novel programs aimed at persistent CF infection.
Infection biology is clear; biofilms NTM and phage manufacturing/regulatory paths are messy. Endpoints exist but chronic infection trials are hard.
Chronic inhaled-antibiotic use remains common among PA-positive patients (tobramycin 51.2% aztreonam 30.3% of ages >=6).
Phage is in a recruiting CF Phase 2. The adult/older CF population has higher NTM. AMR is a general tailwind not a CF-specific proof.
CFRD 19.2% of the transplant-censored complications population and 29.3% of adults. CFF links CFRD to weight loss lung-function decline and increased mortality. Adult-era disease.
Insulin is guideline SoC; ~58% of people with diabetes used CGM. 16.4% of people with CFRD had no treatment noted; non-insulin therapies 8.0%. No CF-specific disease-modifying metabolic approval.
No reviewed industry CF-specific metabolic drug on the map. Academic SGLT2 GLP-1 metformin and related studies plus one bionic-pancreas device. Few programs aimed at a CF-specific product.
Glucose endpoints and CGM are measurable. Whether CFRD needs a CF-specific drug versus generic metabolic agents plus insulin is the open clinical question.
Chronic insulin and CGM imply ongoing resource use. Not a public CF-specific claims total. Do not scale adult CFRD prevalence to a TAM.
Adult-majority Registry (61.6%). Incretin/SGLT2 era plus CGM adoption create a concrete trial window. Modulators did not make CFRD rare.

PERT 80.2% so pancreatic insufficiency remains common. Advanced CFLD is smaller and severe (cirrhosis 2.7%; 861 people; varices 25% among cirrhosis). Combined category mixes a solved product class with a rare severe liver problem.

PERT products exist. CFF recommends against routine UDCA to prevent advanced CFLD. No approved disease-modifying CFLD therapy in the MVP table. Gap is not absence of enzymes; it is residual malabsorption and liver disease.
Two industry GI candidates (ANG003 NHS7108) plus academic constipation/motility repurposing and an approved PERT class. Several programs not none.
Enzyme replacement is tractable. CFLD endpoints and addressable population are messy.
Chronic PERT and supplements. Advanced CFLD care is high-intensity but small N. No public cost build.
Adult GI burden persists after modulators. New lipase candidates are in Phase 2. Not a single dramatic enabling event.
Adults 61.6%; ages 60+ n=1437; survival 65.4 years. Adult anxiety 31.9% depression 30.2% osteopenia 19.4%. Large demographic shift; burden is heterogeneous and not one CF-specific disease.
Screening and generic SoC exist for bone mental health hypertension and cancer. This may be a care-delivery and screening problem more than a missing CF drug.
No reviewed CF-specific therapeutic map asset. Sparse drug pipeline is a fact; empty pipeline is not by itself a company-formation argument.
No single CF-specific target. Cancer CVD bone and mental health are different development problems. Low for a default biotech thesis.
Aging-related care is health-system intensive. Not a quantified CF-product market in public data.
The 2024 Registry documents the adult/older-adult shift including a new aging chapter. Demographic enablement is real even if the product thesis is not.
Mean 3.0 clinic visits (4.3 in 2019). Dornase 80.6% and hypertonic saline 62.6% of ages >=6. Adult-majority population still managing multi-drug regimens. Burden fell and did not disappear.
Telehealth exists (mean 0.4 visits). Pharmacist visits 60.4%. Digital adherence and adult-care capacity remain incomplete. Not an absent-drug problem.
Zero therapeutic map assets. 17 auto-suggested active CF-like care-delivery studies that must not be ranked as products. Few commercial CF-specific services products in the reviewed set.
Digital and care-coordination interventions are feasible. Endpoints (visits PRO exacerbations time-on-therapy) are messy in public Registry data.
Specialty pharmacy and visit volume are utilization proxies only. Services reimbursement in CF is mixed and not a claims-backed MVP input.
Visit volume dropped after 2019 and the population is majority adult. Enabling change is incremental rather than a single new modality.
